scope: demo: 5 shorts tracing the arc of the course (Ax = b -> four subspaces -> least squares -> eigenvalues -> SVD); notes will cover all 41 outline units

series.title: Linear Algebra in Five Pictures
series.audience: curious beginners who know high-school algebra; no prior linear algebra

shorts.title: Two pictures of one system: rows vs columns
shorts.hook: You solved 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3 by crossing two lines. There is a second picture with no lines at all.
shorts.claim: Solving Ax = b means finding the combination of A's columns that lands exactly on b.

worked_example.setup: Strang's first system: 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3. The columns of A are a1 = (2, -1) and a2 = (-1, 2); the target is b = (0, 3).
steps: Row picture: the lines y = 2x and -x + 2y = 3 cross at (x, y) = (1, 2), since -1 + 2*2 = 3.
Column picture: take x = 1 copy of a1, the arrow (2, -1).
Take y = 2 copies of a2: 2*(-1, 2) = (-2, 4).
Add tip to tail: (2, -1) + (-2, 4) = (0, 3), which is exactly b.
worked_example.result: x = 1, y = 2: the same two numbers are the crossing point of the rows and the recipe 1*a1 + 2*a2 = b for the columns.

shorts.visual: One number plane. First the row lines y = 2x and -x + 2y = 3 draw in and meet at the dot (1, 2). Then the lines fade and the column arrows a1 = (2, -1) and a2 = (-1, 2) grow from the origin; a1 stays, a2 stretches to 2*a2 = (-2, 4) and slides tip-to-tail onto the tip of a1, landing on the target dot b = (0, 3). The weights 1 and 2 stay labelled on the arrows and reappear as the coordinates of the old crossing point.
shorts.misconception: Ax is not only rows dotted with x; the same product is a weighted sum of A's columns, and that view keeps working in 10 or 1000 dimensions where crossing lines can no longer be drawn.

practice.question: With the same columns a1 = (2, -1) and a2 = (-1, 2), which combination reaches b = (1, 1)?

shorts.title: What a matrix keeps and what it crushes
shorts.hook: This matrix eats three numbers and returns two. Some input directions vanish completely. Which ones, and how many?
shorts.claim: Rank r splits the input space into an r-dimensional row space that A keeps and an (n - r)-dimensional nullspace that A sends to zero.

steps: Eliminate: row 2 - 2*row 1 = (0, 0, 0), leaving one pivot, so the rank is r = 1.
Free columns 2 and 3 give the special solutions s1 = (-2, 1, 0) and s2 = (-2, 0, 1); A s1 = A s2 = (0, 0), so the nullspace is a plane of dimension n - r = 2.
Both special solutions are perpendicular to the row (1, 2, 2): -2 + 2 + 0 = 0 and -2 + 0 + 2 = 0. The row space is the line through (1, 2, 2), dimension r = 1.
Take x = (-1, 3, 2) = (1, 2, 2) + s1. Then A x = (-1 + 6 + 4, -2 + 12 + 8) = (9, 18), exactly A(1, 2, 2) = (9, 18): the nullspace part was crushed.
Every output is a multiple of (1, 2), so the column space is a line (dimension r = 1) and the left nullspace is the perpendicular line through (2, -1) (dimension m - r = 1).
worked_example.result: Inputs: R3 = row-space line (1) + nullspace plane (2), so 1 + 2 = 3. Outputs: R2 = column-space line (1) + left-nullspace line (1), so 1 + 1 = 2.

shorts.visual: Split screen. Left: R3 with the row-space arrow (1, 2, 2) standing perpendicular to the nullspace plane spanned by s1 and s2. Right: R2 with the column-space line through (1, 2) and the left-nullspace line through (2, -1). The input x = (-1, 3, 2) is drawn as row part + nullspace part; under A the nullspace part shrinks to the origin while the row part lands on (9, 18) on the column-space line. Dimension counters 1 + 2 = 3 and 1 + 1 = 2 stay on screen.
shorts.misconception: The information A destroys is not scattered randomly: all of it lives in one subspace, the nullspace, and that subspace is exactly perpendicular to the rows.

practice.question: Change the last entry: A = [[1, 2, 2], [2, 4, 5]]. What are the rank and the nullspace dimension now?
practice.answer: Row 2 - 2*row 1 = (0, 0, 1), so r = 2 and the nullspace has dimension 3 - 2 = 1, spanned by (-2, 1, 0).

shorts.title: The best-fit line leaves a perpendicular error
shorts.hook: Three points refuse to sit on one line. Which line is best, and why does a right angle decide it?
shorts.claim: The least-squares line is the one whose error vector is perpendicular to every column of A, which is why we solve A^T A x̂ = A^T b.

worked_example.setup: Fit b = C + D t to the points (t, b) = (0, 6), (1, 0), (2, 0). A has columns (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 2); b = (6, 0, 0).
steps: No exact line: t = 0 forces C = 6, then C + D = 0 gives D = -6 but C + 2D = 0 gives D = -3.
Normal equations: A^T A = [[3, 3], [3, 5]] and A^T b = (6, 0), so 3C + 3D = 6 and 3C + 5D = 0.
Subtract: 2D = -6, so D = -3 and C = 5. The best line is b = 5 - 3t.
Projection p = (5, 2, -1); error e = b - p = (1, -2, 1).
worked_example.result: Best line b = 5 - 3t with errors (1, -2, 1) and total squared error 1 + 4 + 1 = 6; the error is perpendicular to both columns.

shorts.visual: Top half: a t-b grid with the three data dots (0, 6), (1, 0), (2, 0) and a line that tilts and slides until it settles on b = 5 - 3t, with vertical error bars of 1 up, 2 down, 1 up staying attached to the dots. Bottom half: the same fit in R3, where the plane of the columns (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 2) holds the shadow p = (5, 2, -1) of the arrow b = (6, 0, 0), and the error arrow e = (1, -2, 1) drops from b to p with a right-angle marker on the plane.
shorts.misconception: Least squares does not minimise the perpendicular distances from the points to the line; it minimises the vertical errors, and the right angle lives in R3 between e and the column space, not on the t-b graph.

practice.question: Fit a least-squares line through (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 0). What are C and D?
practice.answer: A^T b = (3, 3) gives 3C + 3D = 3 and 3C + 5D = 3, so D = 0 and C = 1: the flat line b = 1, with errors (-1, 2, -1).

shorts.title: Why A to the 100th is easy: follow the eigenvectors
shorts.hook: 1000 people shuffle between two cities every year by the same rule. Where does everyone end up, and how fast?
shorts.claim: Each multiplication by A rescales every eigenvector part by its eigenvalue, so the lambda = 1 part survives and the lambda = 1/2 part halves away.

worked_example.setup: Markov matrix A = [[0.8, 0.3], [0.2, 0.7]]: each year 80% of city 1 stays and 20% moves, 70% of city 2 stays and 30% moves. Start with u0 = (1000, 0).
worked_example.result: The populations approach the steady state (600, 400), and the gap to it halves every year: 400, 200, 100, 50, 25.

shorts.visual: A plane with two fixed eigenvector lines, one through (600, 400) and one along (1, -1). The state dot starts at (1000, 0), drawn as a fixed arrow (600, 400) plus a sliding arrow 400*(1, -1). Each year tick the sliding arrow halves while the fixed arrow never moves, and the dot hops (800, 200) -> (700, 300) -> (650, 350) -> (625, 375) toward the steady state. Two city bars at the side show the same numbers.
shorts.misconception: The long-run split does not depend on how the 1000 people start out; only the lambda = 1 eigenvector survives, and a different start only changes how big the decaying part is.

practice.question: Start instead with u0 = (0, 1000). What is u1, and where does the population settle?
practice.answer: u1 = A(0, 1000) = (300, 700), and it still settles at (600, 400).

shorts.title: Every matrix turns a circle into an ellipse
shorts.hook: Feed a matrix every arrow on a circle. However messy the matrix, out comes a clean ellipse. Why?
shorts.claim: Every matrix sends some pair of perpendicular unit vectors v1, v2 to perpendicular vectors sigma1 u1 and sigma2 u2; that pair is the SVD, A = U Sigma V^T.

worked_example.setup: A = [[6, 8], [-4, 3]] acting on the unit circle, with the perpendicular unit vectors v1 = (0.6, 0.8) and v2 = (-0.8, 0.6).
steps: The ordinary axes get skewed: A(1, 0) = (6, -4) and A(0, 1) = (8, 3), whose dot product is 48 - 12 = 36, so they are no longer perpendicular.
Singular values sigma1 = 10 and sigma2 = 5; check: A^T A = [[52, 36], [36, 73]] has eigenvalues 100 = 10^2 and 25 = 5^2.
Area check: |det A| = |18 + 32| = 50 = sigma1 * sigma2.
worked_example.result: A = U Sigma V^T with U = I, Sigma = diag(10, 5) and V = [v1 v2]: the unit circle becomes an ellipse with semi-axes 10 and 5.

shorts.visual: Left: the unit circle with two highlighted perpendicular arrows v1 = (0.6, 0.8) and v2 = (-0.8, 0.6) and the standard axes in grey. The whole circle morphs under A into an ellipse on the right: the grey axes land on the skewed pair (6, -4) and (8, 3), while the highlighted arrows land on (10, 0) and (0, 5), exactly the ellipse's long and short axes, with a right-angle marker kept on the highlighted pair throughout.
shorts.misconception: Singular values are not eigenvalues: this A has complex eigenvalues (no real direction keeps its line), yet sigma1 = 10 and sigma2 = 5 are real and positive.
